contentHtml:
In this article, Dr Naga Suresh Veerapu, Associate Professor, School of Natural Sciences, Shiv Nadar University, Delhi - NCR highlights how host genetics can significantly influence the severity and outcome of Ebola and other infectious diseases, shaping immune response, viral susceptibility, recovery and survival. 

The influence of host genetics on infectious disease outcomes goes beyond Ebola virus disease. Individuals infected with the same pathogen often show markedly different clinical outcomes. Research on diseases like COVID-19, influenza, HIV, tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and malaria shows that host genetic diversity greatly affects the body’s response to infection. These studies indicate that variability in disease outcomes is a common feature of infectious diseases. It results from the complex ways in which germs and a person’s genes interact.

The Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo showed how hard it is to predict how Ebola affects people. Out of 3,605 confirmed and probable cases, 1,597 people died (44%), 626 recovered, and some exposed individuals had few or no symptoms. These different outcomes raise a key question in infectious disease biology: Why can such a deadly virus quickly shut down organs and kill some individuals, yet allow others to recover, while leaving others with only mild or asymptomatic infection? While age, the amount of virus, and preexisting health conditions matter, they don’t explain why people react so differently.

Growing evidence suggests that part of the answer lies in the host’s genes. In the past ten years, research has shown that a person’s genetic makeup is important in how their body responds to Ebola infection. Genetic traits can affect how the virus enters cells, how the immune system acts, and how the body heals itself. As a result, the outcome of Ebola infection depends not only on how dangerous the virus is, but also on the person’s genetic risk and their ability to fight off the infection.

Differences in host genes affect many important pathways that help control Ebola infection. Changes in genes related to both innate and adaptive immunity can change how well the immune system recognizes the virus, starts antiviral defenses, and limits how much the virus can multiply. Virus variants that affect interferon signaling, cytokine production, and inflammation can determine whether the body fights off the virus or damages itself by overreacting, leading to blood vessel damage, organ failure and death. Also, genetic differences in proteins required for the virus to enter cells, such as the Niemann–Pick C1 (NPC1) receptor, can affect how readily Ebola infects cells.

Host genetics also influences pathways that control blood vessel health and blood clotting, which are both seriously affected in severe Ebola cases. Differences in genes that regulate how blood vessels work, how blood clots, and how the body responds to inflammation may help explain why some people get severe bleeding while others have less severe symptoms. Studies of Ebola survivors and people with no symptoms have identified natural genetic variants that may boost antiviral immunity, help clear the virus, or reduce harmful inflammation, thereby improving survival.

Together, these findings have changed our understanding of Ebola virus disease. It is now seen as shaped by both the virus and the person’s genes. By identifying the genes that influence risk, resistance, and disease severity, researchers are seeking new ways to treat patients, assess risk, and develop better vaccines and treatments. More generally, Ebola is now a key example for studying how human genetic differences affect the outcomes of infectious diseases, offering lessons that apply to other diseases as well.
